text:
Help me write a case for my promotion. I'm the assistant front office manager at a 180-room hotel, and the front office manager job is open. I'm applying, and my general manager wants it in writing by Friday.

Facts:
- I've worked here 6 years, the last 2 as assistant manager.
- Our guest score for check-in on the main review site went from 7.9 to 8.6 over the last 18 months. The lobby and all the rooms were renovated during the same time.
- I rewrote the front desk training. New hires now work the desk alone after 5 shifts instead of 9.
- Front desk turnover was 9 of 14 people in the year before I became assistant manager, and 5 of 14 last year.
- I've covered the front office manager's job alone for the 7 weeks since she left.
- I have never managed a budget. The front office manager owns a $1.1 million payroll budget.

I want it to say I'm the main reason our guest scores went up. One page.

Before I draft, here's the plan and one problem with the main claim. A promotion case only gets one reading from your GM, so it's worth agreeing on these first.

## The argument as I'd build it

- **Claim:** You should be promoted to front office manager.
- **Who decides:** Your GM. They know the hotel, they know about the renovation, and they've watched you run the department for 7 weeks.
- **Evidence:**
  - Front desk turnover went from 9 of 14 to 5 of 14. That's 64% down to 36%, so you're losing about half as many people.
  - New hires work the desk alone after 5 shifts instead of 9, which is 44% faster. If last year's 5 departures were each replaced, that's about 20 fewer training shifts a year.
  - You've done the job alone for 7 weeks.
  - The check-in score went from 7.9 to 8.6.
- **The link between evidence and claim:** The best predictor of how someone will do a job is how they've already done it. You've done it for 7 weeks, and you've improved the things the job is responsible for.
- **The objection the GM will raise:** You've never managed a budget, and this role owns $1.1M in payroll.
  - **The answer:** Your two biggest results are payroll results. Turnover and training time are where front desk payroll money gets wasted. The case pairs that with a concrete offer, for example working through the payroll budget with the GM or controller in your first 90 days.
- **How strongly to word it:** Say flatly that you're ready, but qualify the guest score claim (see below).

## The problem with "I'm the main reason scores went up"

- **What you want to say:** You're the main reason check-in scores rose.
- **What your facts support:** The score rose in the same period as your training and retention changes, and also in the same period as a full lobby and room renovation.
- **How your GM will read it:** "The lobby was a construction site and is now brand new. Of course check-in scores went up." Your GM approved that renovation and will think of it first. If the page claims the credit for itself, the GM will start doubting the other numbers too, and those are your strongest ones.

**My recommendation:** Claim a share of the credit, not the main credit. For example: "Check-in scores rose from 7.9 to 8.6. The new lobby helped. So did a desk that kept its people, and new hires who were ready in 5 shifts instead of 9." The GM can't argue with that, and it still connects the score to your work.

**What could support the stronger claim**, if you have any of it:
- The score started rising before the lobby was finished.
- The check-in score rose more than the room or cleanliness scores.
- Review comments name your staff or mention fast, friendly check-in.

## Before I write, I need to know

1. Do you want the shared-credit version or the "main reason" version? It's your call. I'd advise the shared-credit one unless you have something from the list above.
2. In the past 7 weeks, have you handled scheduling, overtime, labor costs or approving payroll? Even partly? If so, that's the best answer to the budget objection.
3. Does anything in those 7 weeks stand out, like a busy stretch, a problem you fixed or a new hire you trained?

When you answer, I'll write the one-page version.

1. Shared-credit is fine; I just want it to say what I actually did. One thing from your list: the renovation started 5 months into those 18 months, and the check-in score had already gone from 7.9 to 8.2 before it started.

2. Yes. I've handled scheduling and overtime for the 7 weeks. Overtime came in under the monthly plan.

3. In those 7 weeks, no front desk shift went uncovered. Nothing else really stands out.

I've written it as the shared-credit version. Because the score went from 7.9 to 8.2 before the renovation began, 0.3 of the 0.7 gain came first. You can claim that part without overreaching.

<final_document>
**To:** [GM name]
**From:** [Your name], Assistant Front Office Manager
**Re:** Application for Front Office Manager

I'm applying for the Front Office Manager position. I've been doing this job on my own for the past seven weeks, and I'd like to keep doing it.

**The last seven weeks**

Since [previous manager's name] left, I've run the front office by myself, including scheduling and overtime. Every front desk shift has been covered in that time, and overtime has come in under the monthly plan.

**What I've changed in two years as assistant manager**

- **Turnover.** In the year before I became assistant manager, 9 of our 14 front desk staff left. Last year, 5 left. We used to lose almost two-thirds of the desk each year. Now we keep almost two-thirds.
- **Training.** I rewrote our front desk training. New hires now work the desk alone after 5 shifts instead of 9. Replacing last year's five departures took about 20 fewer training shifts than it would have under the old program.
- **Guest scores.** Our check-in score on [review site] rose from 7.9 to 8.6 over the last 18 months. The new lobby helped. But almost half of that gain, from 7.9 to 8.2, happened in the five months before the renovation started. That part of the improvement came from the people at the desk: a team that stays, and new hires who are ready sooner.

**The budget**

I haven't managed a budget, and this role owns a $1.1 million payroll budget. I don't want to downplay that. But most of my work over the past two years has been on the parts of that budget the desk can control. Turnover and training time are where front desk payroll gets spent twice, on the person who left and again on the person who replaces them. For the last seven weeks I've also managed scheduling and overtime against plan, and stayed under it.

To close the gap, I propose going through the full payroll budget with you [or: our controller] in my first 90 days, line by line. After that, I'd like a monthly review with you so you can see exactly how I'm tracking.

**Why me**

I've worked here for six years. I know this team, our guests and how this desk runs, because I've been running it. If you promote me, nothing needs to be handed over. The department simply keeps running the way it has for the past seven weeks. A new manager from outside would need time to learn a team that has only recently become stable.

I'd welcome the chance to talk this through before you decide.

[Your name]
</final_document>

Before you send it, please check these:

- **Placeholders:** Fill in the brackets: your GM's name, the previous manager's name, the review site, and whether the budget review would be with the GM or the controller.
- **"20 fewer training shifts":** I assumed each of last year's 5 departures was replaced. If any weren't, change the number or cut the sentence.
- **Training timing:** I didn't say the training rewrite happened before the renovation, because you didn't tell me when it happened. If it was in place during those first five months, add that to the guest scores point. It makes your claim to the 7.9→8.2 rise even stronger.
- **Overtime figure:** If you know how far under plan overtime came in, as a dollar amount or a percentage, add it. A number will carry more weight with the GM than "under plan."
